⚠️ **<!-- xtask:begin maturity:titled -->Alpha<!-- xtask:end -->.** sprawling <!-- xtask:begin workspace_version -->0.0.13<!-- xtask:end --> ODYSSEY is usable: the resident tools take clearer argument shapes and return denser text, and the city and its configuration now live apart from the binary. It opens a city written by 0.0.12, but the first open can move the city under the home directory, write the `city` configuration line and refresh unedited default prompts. Version 0.0.12 is not promised to read a city that 0.0.13 has written, and the wire moved from WIRE_V 67 to 70, so an old browser tab is refused rather than misread. Before replacing an installed binary, stop the city and verify a restored pre-update backup using the [update guide](https://github.com/2youg1/sprawling-agents/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md#updating).

⚠️ **<!-- xtask:begin maturity:titled -->Alpha<!-- xtask:end -->。** sprawling <!-- xtask:begin workspace_version -->0.0.13<!-- xtask:end --> ODYSSEY 已经可用：常驻工具的参数形状更清楚、返回文字更紧凑，城市和配置文件也与二进制分开放置。它能打开 0.0.12 写下的城市，但第一次打开可能把城市搬到家目录、写入 `city` 配置行，并刷新未改过的默认提示词。0.0.12 不保证能读 0.0.13 写过的城市；协议从 WIRE_V 67 升到 70，旧标签页会被明确拒绝而不是读错。替换已安装的二进制前，请先停止城市，并按[更新指南](https://github.com/2youg1/sprawling-agents/blob/main/docs/getting-started.zh-CN.md#更新)验证更新前备份能恢复。

**What this version is for / 这一版做什么** — in the author's words, below in Chinese and then in English: why tool design balances machine cost against model context, why ownership means predictable behaviour and control, why multi-agent work is primarily a cost problem, and why the last 10% of maintenance still matters. The release also moves the city's default location and configuration format, versions the tool-result renderer, and adds prompt and tool-exposure controls.

**Windows signing / Windows 签名** — The Windows binary of this release is still not signed. The release workflow already signs it through SignPath as soon as the SignPath Foundation issues the project's certificate; see the [Code signing policy](https://github.com/2youg1/sprawling-agents#code-signing-policy). 本版 Windows 二进制仍未签名。发布流程已经接好 SignPath，SignPath Foundation 为本项目签发证书之后就会签名；见[代码签名政策（Code signing policy）](https://github.com/2youg1/sprawling-agents#code-signing-policy)。

欢迎来到sprawling v0.0.13 Alpha 261026 (ODYSSEY)！
这个版本整理了几件常驻工具的输入值和返回值，以及随之改动的工具描述：read、search、tool 与所有拒绝的返回值改成了文本（read 的行号从 1 数起、首行和每 10 行标一个行号，拒绝只占一行），search 收 ripgrep 语法的 `pattern` 与 `output_mode`，只给 `glob` 时按文件名找文件，edit 收 `file_path`／`old_string`／`new_string` 与可选的 `replace_all`、不再要 `base_version`，`plan finish` 收一个路径，`describe` 与 `call` 合并成一件 `tool`；exec 收 `command` 或 `python`，它与连接器的返回值仍是 JSON。这建立在目前只有Claude Code，CodeX，Cursor有充足的优质编程数据且最好的编程模型正来自于这些实验室这个假设理念之上。当然，现在Gemini和Muse都追上来了，但考虑到它们依然是Anthropic和OpenAI的大客户，我依然不觉得有必要关注Muse Code/Antigravity，甚至一定程度上来说即使Cursor现属于XAI（XSI）旗下，Grok Build依然不在我的考虑范围之内。人们说大模型在自家实验室的harness中训练因而表现最好（但这里有些误区：1，实际上这些Harness一天几十上百个Commit，就算只看工具面也并非稳定环境。2，基于单一环境训练会导致模型过拟合特定环境，聪明模型会自适应各种环境以多种方式达成目标），所以我想让更多模型（即非Claude/GPT/Grok）的表现更好，那么就让AX面接近Claude Code/CodeX/Cursor即可。正如它们自己也不稳定，所以我也不能说去copy它们的某天的某个快照版本，反过来目前也没有任何一个实验室说自己的harness取得了对某个模型在某一类任务上的最优解，同时这三个harness很明显它们的内置工具/工具描述/调用格式和返回值并非一模一样，**没有什么绝对权威/最佳实践**，因而只能说对于任务完成的能力做了一部分优化。但这个版本没有重写内置提示词：City.md（类似于每个Harness的内置提示词）本版一字未改；本版做的是把 City.md、MAYOR.md、CLERK.md 的默认文字收归二进制（城里没改过的旧副本开城时换成新默认，改过的原样保留），并按新的 edit 合约改写了 Mayor 的规程，措辞基本没动，这些提示词的优化会在接下来的几个版本进行。另外一边我也在想要不要提供一些内置提示词（类似于Hermes内置了一些Prompt人格），考虑到目前一个新用户下载sprawling agent之后可能要迁移/新写不少提示词（当然正如之前我说过的，类似于告诉模型你是一个编程专家/算法工程师这件事并不会让它们在该领域表现更好，就反过来从训练数据想一想，算法工程师在处理算法问题所以是算法工程师，而不是不断声明这件事）。这个版本同步开始了一个长期的深入打磨工具的计划，早期目标是优化几个常驻工具的返回时间，大家可以在对应的分支里面看到实际的情况，可能会涉及将内容用Zig实现（仅限于小组件用于挤压极限性能），但内核会确保始终保持在Rust。随着我对于更深入地调优积累经验以及模型的进步，性能问题将被更快地解决。人们常说不要自顾自地把理想加到他人身上，他人没义务承担你的一厢情愿，更没责任安抚你的幻灭。我估算了一下：假如我真的将Read工具打磨到了在99%的场景耗时接近当时测得的I/O与必要路径检查的下限（不是每次都真的碰磁盘），能比上个版本的情况节省出多少时间呢？假设是3ms→1ms（这是假设：本版还没有发版构建的读数，等待下一次benchmark测试），即收益需要500次read才会放大到1s，30000次放大到1min。就算是重度Agent开发（例如每个月投入1k$于AI订阅）这个read工具优化每周为你节省的时间也不够你读完这个自然段，但如果完成95%任务所需要频繁调用的工具都得到了极致的优化，且一些工具有更大的优化空间，每个Session相比于目前提速数秒完全可能，同时更重要的是RAM节省和**任务成功率上升**。这里的几秒提速完全有可能会在未来的沙箱引入之后成倍吐出去。现在已经有几层隔离：python 臂跑在 WASI guest 里（本版起每个进程只编译一次，内存上限就是 run 的上限），exec 可以在沙箱副本里跑（按工具一份、每条命令前同步），Windows 上 run 的进程树挂在 Job Object 下。在我的设想中，接下来要做的是按需为Agent执行exec时提供一个一次性简易沙箱。我们总听到说“给你的Agent一个沙箱”，甚至有些Agent一开始就在沙箱里，所有的云服务平台都推出了自己的Agent沙箱……那这个按需的一次性沙箱到底怎么做呢？这是我没想清楚因而必须延后的事情。而且不同模型需要沙箱的程度也完全不同，比如说Claude完全有可能不需要沙箱的时候它就去用了沙箱因为它认为这样更安全，然后一些模型完全有可能直接忽视沙箱在系统盘里做高危行动。已经有一个浏览器（假设WebUI）在项目外成为常驻RAM开销了（就像构建桌面程序用Electron框架自带的内存开销），我们还需要多少加法呢？做一个有品味的设计不是选什么元素来好的组合，而是不选什么好的元素来组合，就是说“这个很好，但我不需要”，以及一些时候说“你们都说这个很好，我认为这不好”。工具优化对所有Harness都差不多分成两部分：1，机器运行时。2，Agent上下文。前者要求返回的速度越快越好，运行时的RAM/SSD开销越低越好，后者则是不断调整工具描述和工具回复。工具描述的目的是让模型知道什么时候用和怎么用的同时越短越好（所以说有些模型在自家的Harness表现最好，因为它并不需要任何工具描述就可以知道有哪些工具和该如何调用工具，因而理论上上下文成本可以降低到极致），工具回复则是让回传内容无限接近一维格式化文本（Markdown/XML/TOML……），实际上不少工具的返回值依然保持着面向终端中的人类，它既不是高信息密度的图片也不能“逐行”阅读（即像LLM那样阅读），那么优化的方向也就自然是要么压成一维格式化文本，要么快速整理后以图片形式回传（不少模型在长文阅读上图片的Token开销少于纯文字，但复杂任务成功率是否会下降仍未可知，而如果模型看到图片之后还在思考Token中进行OCR反而会导致额外的开销）。本版最大的优化之一是把城和配置文件从二进制所在的文件夹里分了出来：没指名的城住在 `~/sprawling/city`，每份配置文件可以带一个 `format` 编号，比二进制新的文件会被拒并提示升级，旧的由开城时的迁移阶梯带到当前格式，原件先备份到 `~/.sprawling/backups/`；默认提示词文字归二进制，人改过的副本不动。这样未来版本产生Breaking Change的概率应当能降低（本版阶梯还是空的，三种文件都还在 format 1），当然我在这个版本的声明应该保守一些，是否能减少Breaking Change需要下个版本确定，目前的希望是自下版开始到v0.1.0beta乃至以后都不出现任何Breaking change，让Breaking change成为需要声明的意外而非默认标注。
之前我们谈到了harness的黑箱问题，我们进一步想想什么是“你的harness”？如果这意味着你需要精通harness的设计与编程（以及有充足token）来“开箱”，一定程度上这就不算“你的harness”。每一个组件都可以替换这点不错，sprawling agents可以做到，但我不卖token，我不想止步于此。从ax和ux的角度来想一想，我可以在任何一个工作区（楼）自定义system prompt：楼可以有自己的 City.md 替换城的那份，每个模型可以有城级或楼级的额外 prompt，楼根以下每一级房间的 AGENTS.md 都会进前缀，加载哪些skill/mcp也由楼决定（本版已经可以按全城或本楼调整工具的三档暴露，并在楼页的能力节编辑这些设置；工具描述覆盖仍留给后面的版本），且尽可能所有的修改不消耗token，这样足够“完全掌握”一个harness了吗？归根结底什么是“所有权”？在罗马法中，它意味着对物的绝对支配∶使用，售卖，毁灭……现在我们购入一款软件，一个绑定软件的硬件，我们更像是租用而非拥有它。的确理论上厂家会把它的体验优化到极致，至于我们也不会去做哪些它们不提供给我们的内容，但现实不是理论，以打印机举例，不少打印机强制联网检查订阅并审查打印内容，当然最重要的是审查你是否添加官方油墨，遇到“问题”只能官方收费报修。我有一个工具，我对它的想法是它不会有我不想有的行为并允许我做我认为可以的行为，也就是**可预测性**。自由/隐私地使用，可预测的行为，以及自定义的权利，我认为这是我所有的工具应有的特质。如果我想把sprawling agents变成你觉得“我所有”的agent，我要做的是比如说把license换成CC0吗？或者写一本书讲一下如何使用sprawling agents（其实现在已经有一些出版物在教如何使用Codex，但正如前面所说Codex一天可不止发一个rc，这些书写完还没排到印刷可能对应的功能就变了）？我想这两种做法都不会让它更属于你，而且某种程度上来说sprawling agents是一个“distinctive” harness∶一方面我在讨论更高的自由度/可定制化/上下文透明性，一方面我又在讨论隐私/安全/性能，然后设计上我还在讨论反注意力和无聊，后台则针对长程任务与大规模agent协作调优……没有预算锁，不能关闭加密，不会弹出内置模板和工作建议，不做内置记忆，甚至没有云同步账号系统（无疑是优点）……这是个复杂的难题，我讨论它并不是说有最终的答案，而是公开透明地说正在思考这方面的问题，就像没有办法满足所有人（一定程度上包括自己），很多问题之间本身就互斥自然也没办法满足。不过让sprawling agents的行为更加可预测并不是不能做到的事情，只要我不断推进**可观测性的提升**，你就更有可能获得充足的信息以更好地预测Agent的行为，定位运行时问题的根源并做出针对性优化。对于云端Agent问题，经过对Oracle和cloudflare的免费额度的调研，可以说它们足够非开发场景下的全部工作，前者的VPS有着极度慷慨的运存与流量，后者用隧道或边缘接入很方便（静态网站托管不等于能跑整座城市），因而将其设计为sprawling agent的理想工作环境（而非标准或推荐，意味着依然希望能在非常差的设备上高速运行,尤其是我非常想让sprawling agents跑在阅读器和流媒体盒子上面）。谈到实际的开发工作，目前开发sprawling agent的机器是i5-1340P+16GB（顺便提一下，按 GitHub 文档，公开仓库的标准 Linux runner（`ubuntu-latest`）是 4 核 16 GB，私有仓库是 2 核 8 GB；1 核 5 GB 的是 `ubuntu-slim` 单核 runner，跑在容器里，单个 job 限时 15 分钟），真实开发场景下除非有1-2GB RAM的差异，不然大部分Harness本身的性能差异对于编译器或其他工具的性能开销而言**几乎可以忽略不计**。假设sprawling agent比某个其它Harness在read工具上快了10ms，在可能要跑10min的一次Cargo Build面前二者表现差异完全可以忽略（也不是每个场景都可以忽略，为什么Sprawling Agent选择了Rust作为后端而不是比如说Go这样迭代更快且有垃圾回收器的语言，一方面是内存安全；另一方面是垃圾回收器带来的运行时内存与CPU开销，以及在高分配率、长尾延迟敏感场景里可能出现的问题（Go的GC大部分工作与程序并发执行，这里真正要比较的是分配率、堆目标、p99/p999与常驻内存）。编译器这种大部分时候跑数分钟的场景那完全可以忽略，但如果任务本身是大规模的高频率数百毫秒的工作，那某一个不幸的任务就会被明显拖慢。最重要是我觉得Rust本身非常适合AI，因为模型写出来的东西能立刻被编译器、clippy、格式化与测试验证，而那些新设计出来适合AI的语言没有如此多的训练资料/工具链/稳定性，所谓的适合AI思路却和Rust差不多为什么不直接Rust。很难理解为什么有些人认为Rust编译器不能发现所有问题就感觉它本身没什么价值，吸尘器比起扫把无疑是升级，你用吸尘器不能制造无尘室用扫把也不能，吸尘器可以让你更轻松达成用心扫干净的情况这不是进步吗？其实Vibe Coding也是相同的道理，似乎24年之前世界上到处都是优雅的代码，没有运行时奔溃，安全泄露，技术债，烂尾项目，外包开发……大部分人遇到错误只看官方文档就能推出最佳实践，不需要Google到长期无人维护的论坛看经验分享。如果你过去能写出高质量的代码现在也可以，AI没有从你身上吸取灵魂。如果你不会长期维护一个项目现在也不会，AI不会自动给你发一份维护项目的工资。AI是工具，Rust也是工具，过去你不在终端里手写汇编而是思考实现方案现在也如此）。
然后是multi-agent的部分。在sprawling-agents设计的早期我思考过多种方案，但最终选择了目前这种**约等于0方案**。当然最重要的考虑当然是多Agent编排**99%可以用SKILL解决**，没有必要写代码，你可以为任何你需要面对的工作设立一个专门的工作区然后设计专门的Workflow，并在里面教会你的Agent怎么编排，只要它们能知道自己目前处在什么位置就行。因此这个方向上我最早的做法也就是写了一个SKILL，要求主Agent给每个子Agent一个可以告诉它其位置和任务的编号并写一个markdown解释清楚，现在的JOB.md与URBANITE.md就是这个思路的延申。把Prompt→Loop→Graph倒过来看（不关心X上面的网红或者一些卖课营销的话），其实实战效果的提升来自于模型能力的提升本质都是Prompt Engineering，实践中产生的情况无非Human Prompting 父Agent→父Agent Prompting 子Agent→子Agent Prompting 孙Agent……子子孙孙无穷匮也，过去是人把大任务拆分小任务和检查点当协调者，现在是Agent自己拆分自己协调自己修正。一些完全脱离模型发展现实的“理想”方案的辨析能力我感觉就是我在这个探索过程中最大的收获：比如说7月Claude给Sprawling agents的设计就很“模拟人生”，给每个Agent一堆属性，甚至建立社群系统，个人权重，信誉积分（社会信用）等。问题来了，我现在看到的很多模型，标称上下文已经到1M，但**有效上下文往往远低于标称**，激活参数越来越小，缓存寿命也因提供商与产品而异，从性能和成本上来说这个方案都没有任何可取之处。这也是Personal Agent最大的问题，它们怎么管理上下文和计算KV Cache的价格?在我看来只有10M有效上下文+24h缓存我们才应该使用这种持久化方案。从7月甚至更早到现在，一个Agent超过有效上下文必须开新Agent之后我怎么让后一个Agent成为之前的Agent这个问题从来没有解决过，现存的任何记忆方法都只是把本就不够透明的上下文变得更加黑箱，因而我在sprawling agents中反过来选择了最不黑箱的Markdown+Jsonl方案。这绝不是性能最优的方案，甚至任何情况下都不能算作优秀的方案，但考虑到目前Multi-Agent方法的混乱环境，也没有谁说自己的方案就一定能比纯Markdown+Jsonl更性能且更经济。Arxiv上面有大量相关的论文，我也有不定期跟进相关的研究（虽然大部分论文我只看第一页），可目前还没有任何一个方案能说服我放弃当前方案(我之前讨论过两期论文单后面我的想法改观了，首先就不能确保全方面提升，最核心是我没有必要用代码去实现Workflow，不如直接推荐几个开源SKILL)。当然这也不是说multi-agent的发展毫无进展，相反进步很大：Multi-Agent的成本在快速降低，尤其是部分缓存可复用后基于/fork的自分裂扇出后，原本随分支与重复上下文快速膨胀的成本，至少有机会被压到更接近一次函数的水平。单Agent能力因为有效上下文的进展缓慢导致能力边界只能随着Token效率缓慢提升，而模型智力的不断发展又导致人们必须不断寻找那些更困难的任务，这才是Multi-Agent各种方案真正的竞争之处——**成本控制**。任何模型实验室都没有主动推动Multi-Agent成本下降的动机，因为Workflow和模型能力不同，大部分实验室的Harness都已经开源，表现良好的方案会在1天内快速扩散，那些真正对大部分用户重要的Workflow是将大型任务成本降低到极致（其实一定程度上来说聪明的模型也会自己探索协作方案，但**探索过程也是成本**，直接将一个局部最优写成SKILL复用少量大任务而言更加经济，不过如果你有数百万美元我当然很推荐你深入探索一下写篇论文，说不定还能成立一家公司。但sprawling的设计不是提供这个workflow，我没有充足的财力针对每个模型测试数T Token并定制最优Workflow（如果我是Cursor工程师就可以，但某种程度上来说一到两个最高档订阅的周额度，无论是GPT还是Claude都够探索一个私人业务/专业领域Workflow，但这也只是前80%，后续的迭代和维护，以及专业人士的监督，真实场景的反馈才是最大的成本），所以Sprawling agents的目标是提供一个好的平台用于个人搭建并测试自己的Workflow。我来处理大规模运行恼人的性能问题，减少运行时的黑箱问题，你用你的专业知识和真实场景专注研发最适合你的Workflow。sprawling agents默认的设计是一个相对去中心化的方案，模型在写域、准入门和保密边界之内**尽量自由**（反过来作为观测入口的mayor实际上没有任何自由，请你把mayor的设计当作一个转接口，它专注于告诉你必要的信息以及传达你的想法，这也是我专家和沟通分离想法的设计意图，目前的模型都有把能力控制在你实际的能力附近的倾向，当然这其实是因为LLM本质是一维Token序列预测函数，如果有个转接层就可以允许把你的想法先翻译成专业的内容去执行，然后再让mayor翻译回“姥姥也能听懂的语言”，这样用一点额外成本实现沟通和任务完成能力的双赢。在这里我说的是一点额外成本，因为你其实可以用一个很便宜的模型当Mayor，并给这个模型登记一个较小的上下文窗口（例如256k，`select_model` 的 `context_tokens`，上下文提醒按它量；这是对模型的设置，不是 Mayor 席位单独的上限），或者用deepseek这种接近24h缓存的模型，这样后台工作专注于一次性完成任务即可，减少沟通时缓存重算风险），因为任何的预先限制都会成为你定制的阻碍。
我相信我们每天用的软件现在除了AI按钮之外有不少新功能背后的代码主体已经迈向100%AI，甚至几乎所有的大厂AI相关产品的绝大多数代码现在都由Agent生成（如果你是一个AI实验室领导人你发现自己的员工在手写产品，大概会有1弗朗克时间感激他的匠人精神，剩下的1天会沉浸在自己的模型弱得没法开发自家产品的绝望中，想象一下[将Bun从Zig迁移到Rust时用了预发布版Claude Fable 5](https://bun.com/blog/bun-in-rust)，今年早些时候它已经能让五十来个动态workflow连续跑十一天，这是多少个月的差距）。要我说除非你是抱着玩游戏充值一样的心态，否则你**绝对不该许愿式编程**，许愿式编程可以让模型做出很好看的Demo，但几乎不会成为被长期使用的项目，严格来说如果你不理解你所设计的东西，那么目前还没被AI加速到极致的软件开发最后10%你也不会愿意去走（现在不少项目管生不管养，甚至火了的项目也有出现热度一过马上停止维护），某种程度上你甚至也不会愿意长久去用。其实这个就像现在大逆向时代诞生的各种项目，的确一个付费功能被解决了，但大公司的护城河并不在产品上（现在越来越多大公司拥抱开源也是如此），它们的算力、宣发、售后、资本、生态、习惯、社区……这些才是开源维护者最难获取的东西。反而功能这种灵感性的创造更容易被大公司剽窃，正如我们历史上一次又一次看到的。如果一个我需要的开源项目作者因为现实问题无法维护，而我又不愿意fork后维护或重造轮子，那最后的赢家就是几乎有着无限成本的大厂。过去到现在，我们依然没办法完美确保没有bug、兼容性问题，AI让个人开发者维护项目的成本在降低，但投入精力并没有多少降低，Theo3这样的大网红投入数万美元将tsc用Rust重构之后都说自己并不准备维护。sprawling agent v0.0.1的“本体”是几万字的Markdown，包含了大量设想场景和细节描述，当然当时的模型并没有完全落实它也没有把全部的东西记录下来（不少在我脑子里，但这些在我脑子里的东西会让接下来的开发少走一些弯路），无论什么时候你问我sprawling agents v0.0.1能不能用我都会说试都别试。在此之后的每个版本我都学到了新的东西，进而深入更多细节进行优化，模型和我的工作流也都在发展，所以我制定了一个面向0.1.0Beta的目标（直到我说这是一个不错的Harness，有这么久的维护可以试一下之后我才会打上这个Beta的Tag）来让sprawling agents真的推荐使用。现在Demo和作品的差异其实也就只在最后的10%之内，但体验上的差别就像0和1，无数细节处理和优化（以及bug修复）才能让一个项目显得像刚刚从0走到1（目前我判断sprawling agent走到大概0.6）。最近Typescript生态中大量基于Claude Opus5.5重写的tsc出现，我也在考虑这些项目的表现，等有更加AI Native且性能极致的前端生态完善之后再推进生成式UI，不过目前直接写Svelte+CSS+JavaScript的方案大体已经相对固定了，其实一定程度上来说默认组件或模板的方案总体上表现会更快一些，但模型的成长速度那么快，每个人的品味又不一，更加开放自由也许会更好一些。目前项目的前端是Svelte+Typescript的方案，但当我认为前端已经调节到一个比较好的结构时，也有可能会顺应目前的风潮把浏览器客户端换成原生GUI，比如说用[GPUI](https://docs.rs/gpui/latest/gpui/)把前端又迁移回Rust（它目前仍是pre-1.0，官方写着macOS/Linux，Windows支持得先解决；最早项目就用Dioxus做前端，不过依然保留使用[Topcoat](https://github.com/tokio-rs/topcoat)留在WebUI中，因为我转移到Typescript生态只是因为其方便AI写和设计以及包管理器，理想依然是Rust尽可能接管一切，不过这些我都准备拖到年末乃至明年初再判断）。当然这不仅需要前端足够精致，而且依赖项解到一定程度也很必要，现在WebUI提供了大量所需要的功能，我在考虑将其纳入进入v0.1.0Beta的条件之一。我最近对https://github.com/ELY-Open-Source/ElyOffice这个项目非常感兴趣，也是这个项目让我开始思考用GPUI，而不是直接用Tauri保留现在的Svelte前端背着系统WebView。真要做GPUI我也更倾向于让它成为wire的第二个客户端，WebUI继续覆盖远程访问，而不是把内核和界面重新绑死。考虑WebUI还有一个原因是TUI目前能用但效果不是那么好（所以不算一个需要维护的界面），未来如果做GUI就可以内置一个终端做更好的工具终端指令可视化，需要大量TUI操作也可以直接用，不喜欢GUI也可以在模拟终端里面用TUI（当然终端也不只是画几行字，VT解析、Unicode、选区、回滚和PTY……）。不过目前还有另一个想法就是让WebUI支持背景放视频（例如壁纸引擎功能）或者更进一步依靠WebGPU做一些更有意思的事情（我知道有些人有和凌波丽或者其它喜欢的动漫角色实时交流的急切需求，当一切成熟之后，界面这一层也许一个版本就能做出来，但下面这些事本身就是另一套完整产品工作：角色身份一致性/记忆持久化、带有音色克隆的全双工语音交互、2D或3D模型控制和渲染、生图/视频模型搭配、以及一个在其它情景没那么重要但在这个方案中极度重要的UI全液态玻璃化）。

我们还有很长的路要走呢，欢迎参与到项目开发和讨论中来。

---

**In English / 英文版**

Welcome to sprawling v0.0.13 Alpha 261026 (ODYSSEY)!

This release tidies the inputs and outputs of several resident tools, together with the tool descriptions that changed with them: `read`, `search`, `tool` and every refusal now return text (`read` counts lines from 1 and marks its first line and every tenth line with a line number; a refusal takes one line); `search` takes a ripgrep-syntax `pattern` and an `output_mode`, and finds files by name when given only a `glob`; `edit` takes `file_path` / `old_string` / `new_string` and an optional `replace_all`, and no longer asks for `base_version`; `plan finish` takes one path; and `describe` and `call` have merged into one `tool`. `exec` takes `command` or `python`, and its answers, like connector answers, are still JSON. This rests on the assumption that, for now, only Claude Code, CodeX and Cursor have enough high-quality programming data, and that the best programming models come from those labs. Gemini and Muse have of course caught up now, but given that they are still major customers of Anthropic and OpenAI, I still see no need to follow Muse Code/Antigravity; indeed, even though Cursor now belongs to XAI (XSI), Grok Build is still outside my consideration. People say a large model performs best in the harness of its own lab because that is where it was trained, but there are some misconceptions here: first, these harnesses receive dozens or hundreds of commits a day, so even the tool surface alone is not a stable environment; second, training against one environment causes a model to overfit it, whereas a smart model adapts to different environments and achieves its goal in different ways. I want more models — ones other than Claude/GPT/Grok — to perform better, so the AX surface only needs to resemble Claude Code/CodeX/Cursor. Since those harnesses are themselves unstable, I cannot say I am copying a snapshot of any one of them from a particular day; conversely, no lab currently says its harness is optimal for a particular model on a particular class of task, and the built-in tools, tool descriptions, invocation formats and return values of these three harnesses plainly are not identical. **There is no absolute authority or best practice**, so I can only say that this version improves part of what makes a model capable of completing a task. The built-in prompts were not rewritten in this version: City.md, which is like each harness's built-in prompt, has not changed by a single character. What the version does is bring the default text of City.md, MAYOR.md and CLERK.md into the binary (when a city opens, an old copy that nobody edited is replaced with the new default, while an edited copy is kept as it is), and rewrite the Mayor's procedure for the new `edit` contract, with the wording otherwise largely unchanged; prompt optimisation will continue over the next few versions. I am also wondering whether to provide some built-in prompts, rather like the prompt personas built into Hermes, since a new user who downloads sprawling agent may currently have to migrate or write quite a few prompts. As I said before, though, telling a model that it is a programming expert or an algorithm engineer does not make it better in that field: think about the training data instead. An algorithm engineer is an algorithm engineer because they work on algorithm problems, not because they keep declaring that they are one.

Alongside this, the version starts a long-term plan to refine the tools in depth. The early goal is to shorten the response time of several resident tools; you can see what is actually happening in the corresponding branches. Some components may be implemented in Zig, but only small components where the last bit of performance is being squeezed out, and the kernel will always remain in Rust. As I gain more experience with deeper tuning and models improve, performance problems will be solved faster. People often say you should not impose your own ideals on others: other people have no obligation to carry your wishful thinking, and no responsibility to soothe your disillusionment. I made an estimate. Suppose I really refined the Read tool until, in 99% of cases, its latency approached the lower bound of the I/O and necessary path checks measured at the time, without actually touching the disk every time. How much time would that save compared with the previous version? Suppose it went from 3 ms to 1 ms — and this is only a hypothesis: this version has no release-build reading yet and is waiting for the next benchmark. The saving would need 500 reads to add up to one second, and 30,000 reads to add up to one minute. Even in heavy Agent development, say spending 1,000 USD a month on AI subscriptions, the time this Read optimisation saves you in a week would not be enough to finish reading this paragraph. But if the tools called frequently in 95% of tasks were all optimised to their limits, and some of them have much more room for improvement, each Session could plausibly become several seconds faster than it is now; more importantly, it could save RAM and **raise the task success rate**. Those few seconds could then be handed back many times over once a sandbox arrives in the future.

There are already several layers of isolation: the Python arm runs in a WASI guest (from this version, each process compiles it only once, and its memory ceiling is the run's ceiling); `exec` can run in a sandbox copy (one per tool, synchronised before every command); and on Windows the process tree of `run` sits inside a Job Object. In my current conception, the next step is to provide a simple, disposable sandbox on demand when an Agent executes `exec`. We hear “give your Agent a sandbox” all the time; some Agents even start inside one, and every cloud service platform has launched its own Agent sandbox. But how exactly should this on-demand, disposable sandbox work? I have not thought that through, so it has to be postponed. Different models also need sandboxes to very different degrees. Claude, for example, might well use a sandbox when it does not need one because it thinks that is safer, while some other model might ignore the sandbox entirely and perform a dangerous operation on the system drive. There is already a browser — assuming the WebUI — sitting outside the project as a standing RAM cost, much like the memory overhead Electron brings when you build a desktop application. How many more additions do we need? A tasteful design is not a matter of choosing which good elements to combine, but of deciding which good elements not to combine: saying “this is good, but I do not need it”, and sometimes “you all say this is good; I think it is not”.

Tool optimisation has roughly two parts in every harness: first, machine runtime; second, Agent context. The first demands the fastest possible responses and the lowest possible RAM and SSD costs while running. The second means continually adjusting tool descriptions and tool replies. A tool description should tell the model when and how to use the tool while staying as short as possible. This is another reason some models perform best in their own harness: they need no tool description to know which tools exist and how to call them, so in theory the context cost can be driven to its minimum. A tool reply should bring the returned content as close as possible to a one-dimensional formatted text such as Markdown, XML or TOML. In fact, many tools still return values designed for a person at a terminal: the result is neither an information-dense image nor something that can be read “line by line” the way an LLM reads. The natural directions, then, are either to compress it into one-dimensional formatted text, or to organise it quickly and return it as an image. For many models, an image of a long document costs fewer tokens than plain text, although whether the success rate on complex tasks would fall is still unknown; and if the model performs OCR in its thinking tokens after seeing the image, that adds cost instead.

One of this version's largest improvements is to separate the city and its configuration files from the folder containing the binary: an unnamed city now lives at `~/sprawling/city`; each configuration file can carry a `format` number; a file newer than the binary is refused with a request to upgrade; an older file is brought up to the current format by the migration ladder when the city opens, after the original is backed up under `~/.sprawling/backups/`; and the default prompt text belongs to the binary, while a copy edited by a person is left alone. This should reduce the chance of a Breaking Change in future versions. The ladder is still empty in this version, and all three file types are still at format 1, so I should be conservative in what I claim here: whether it really reduces Breaking Changes will have to be established in the next version. For now, the hope is that from the next version through v0.1.0 Beta and beyond there will be no Breaking Changes at all, so that one becomes an exception that must be announced rather than the default label.

We talked before about the black-box problem of a harness. Let us go one step further: what is “your harness”? If it means you need to understand the harness's design and programming, and have plenty of tokens, before you can open the box, then to some extent it is not really “your harness”. Every component can be replaced — that is good, and sprawling agents can do it — but I do not sell tokens, and I do not want to stop there. Think about it from the AX and UX angles. You can define a system prompt in any workspace, or building: a building can have its own City.md replacing the city's copy; each model can have an additional prompt at city or building level; the AGENTS.md of every level below the building root down to the room enters the prefix; and the building decides which skills and MCP servers are loaded. This version can already adjust the three exposure tiers of tools city-wide or for one building, and edit those settings in the building page's capabilities section; overriding tool descriptions is still left to a later version. As far as possible, none of these changes consumes tokens. Is that enough to “master a harness completely”?

What, in the end, is “ownership”? In Roman law it means absolute control over a thing: use, sale, destruction, and so on. When we buy a piece of software today, or hardware bound to software, we seem to rent it rather than own it. In theory, of course, the manufacturer will optimise its experience to the limit, and we will not ask it to do anything it does not offer; but reality is not theory. Take printers. Many must connect to the internet to check a subscription and inspect what is printed; above all, they check whether you have added the manufacturer's own ink, and when a “problem” occurs the only option is an official paid repair. What I want from a tool is that it does nothing I do not want, and lets me do what I believe I should be able to do — in other words, **predictability**. Free and private use, predictable behaviour and the right to customise are the qualities I think every tool I own should have.

If I want sprawling agents to become an Agent of which you can say “this is mine”, should I, for example, change its licence to CC0? Or write a book explaining how to use it? There are already publications teaching people how to use Codex, but as I said above, Codex releases more than one RC a day, so by the time such a book reaches print the corresponding features may already have changed. I do not think either approach would make it belong to you more. In a sense, sprawling agents is also a “distinctive” harness: on one side I discuss greater freedom, customisability and context transparency; on another, privacy, security and performance; in design I also discuss resistance to attention capture and to boredom; and in the background I tune for long-horizon tasks and large-scale Agent collaboration. There is no budget lock, encryption cannot be switched off, no built-in templates or work suggestions pop up, there is no built-in memory, and there is not even a cloud-synchronised account system, which is unquestionably an advantage. This is a difficult, complicated problem. I am not discussing it because I have a final answer; I am saying openly that I am still thinking about it. Just as there is no way to satisfy everyone, myself included to some extent, many requirements are mutually exclusive and naturally cannot all be satisfied. Making sprawling agents more predictable, however, is not impossible. As long as I keep improving **observability**, you are more likely to have enough information to predict an Agent's behaviour, find the cause of a runtime problem and tune it deliberately.

For cloud Agents, after looking into Oracle's and Cloudflare's free tiers, I would say they cover all non-development work. Oracle's VPS has exceptionally generous memory and traffic allowances, while Cloudflare makes access through a tunnel or at the edge convenient — hosting a static website is not the same as being able to run an entire city. I therefore think of them as ideal working environments for sprawling agent, not as standards or recommendations: I still want it to run fast on very poor hardware, and I especially want sprawling agents to run on e-readers and streaming boxes.

On actual development work, the machine currently used to develop sprawling agent has an i5-1340P and 16 GB of RAM. Incidentally, according to GitHub's documentation, the standard Linux runner for a public repository, `ubuntu-latest`, has 4 cores and 16 GB, while a private repository gets 2 cores and 8 GB; the 1-core, 5 GB machine is the single-core `ubuntu-slim` runner, which runs in a container and limits one job to 15 minutes. In real development, unless there is a 1–2 GB difference in RAM, the performance cost of the harness itself is **almost negligible** beside that of a compiler or another tool. If sprawling agent were 10 ms faster than another harness at the Read tool, that difference would be entirely lost inside a Cargo build that might take ten minutes. Not every case can be dismissed that way, though. Why did sprawling agent choose Rust for its backend rather than, say, Go, which iterates faster and has a garbage collector? One reason is memory safety. Another is the runtime memory and CPU cost of garbage collection, and the problems it can create at high allocation rates and in tail-latency-sensitive work. Most of Go's GC runs concurrently with the program; the real comparison here is allocation rate, heap target, p99/p999 and resident memory. For a compiler that usually runs for several minutes, the harness difference can certainly be ignored. But if the task itself is a large-scale, high-frequency stream of jobs lasting hundreds of milliseconds each, one unlucky job can be slowed down noticeably.

Most importantly, I think Rust itself suits AI very well, because what a model writes can immediately be checked by the compiler, Clippy, formatting and tests. New languages designed specifically for AI do not have anything like the same volume of training material, tooling or stability; and if their supposedly AI-friendly ideas are much the same as Rust's, why not use Rust directly? I find it hard to understand the argument that Rust has little value because its compiler cannot find every problem. A vacuum cleaner is unquestionably an upgrade over a broom. Neither a vacuum cleaner nor a broom can create a dust-free room, but a vacuum cleaner makes it easier to reach the state you could achieve by sweeping carefully — is that not progress? Vibe coding is much the same. It is as if, before 2024, the world were full of elegant code with no runtime crashes, security leaks, technical debt, abandoned projects or outsourcing disasters, and as if most people could derive best practices from official documentation alone whenever they met an error, without ever searching old, unmaintained forums for hard-won experience. If you could write high-quality code before, you can still do it now; AI has not sucked out your soul. If you did not maintain a project for the long term before, you will not do so now either; AI does not automatically pay you a salary to maintain one. AI is a tool, and Rust is a tool. You used to think through an implementation rather than writing assembly by hand in a terminal, and that is still what you do now.

Then there is the multi-agent part. Early in the design of sprawling-agents I considered several schemes, but eventually chose the current one, which is **approximately zero scheme**. The most important consideration, of course, is that **99% of multi-Agent orchestration can be solved with a SKILL**; there is no need to write code. You can create a dedicated workspace for whatever work you face, design a dedicated Workflow in it, and teach your Agent how to orchestrate the work there, as long as the Agents can tell where they currently are. My earliest approach in this direction was therefore simply to write a SKILL asking the parent Agent to give every child Agent a number that identified its position and task, and to write a Markdown file explaining everything clearly. Today's JOB.md and URBANITE.md extend that idea.

Turn Prompt → Loop → Graph around, and ignore whatever the influencers on X or the people selling courses are saying: the practical improvement that comes from stronger models is still, at bottom, Prompt Engineering. What happens in practice is nothing more than a human prompting a parent Agent, the parent Agent prompting a child Agent, the child Agent prompting a grandchild Agent, and so on without end. In the past a person split a large task into smaller tasks and checkpoints and acted as coordinator; now an Agent splits the work, coordinates it and corrects it itself. I think the greatest thing I gained from this exploration was the ability to examine certain “ideal” schemes that are wholly detached from how models are actually developing. In July, for example, Claude's design for sprawling agents was very much like The Sims: every Agent had a pile of attributes, and there were even community systems, personal weights and reputation scores — social credit, in other words. But here is the problem. Many models I see now advertise a context of 1M, while their **effective context is often far below the advertised figure**; their activated parameter counts keep getting smaller, and cache lifetimes vary by provider and product. In both performance and cost, that scheme has nothing to recommend it.

This is also the biggest problem with a Personal Agent: how does it manage its context, and how does it price the KV cache? In my view, only when we have 10M of effective context and a 24-hour cache should we use that kind of persistent scheme. From July, and indeed earlier, until now, one question has never been solved: after an Agent exceeds its effective context and a new Agent has to be started, how do I make the new Agent become the old one? Every existing memory method only makes an already insufficiently transparent context even more of a black box. In sprawling agents I therefore chose the least black-box answer instead: Markdown plus JSONL. This is certainly not the most performant scheme; in fact, it could not be called an excellent scheme in any circumstances. But given the confused state of multi-Agent methods today, nobody has demonstrated that their own scheme is necessarily more performant and more economical than plain Markdown plus JSONL either. arXiv has a large body of related research, which I follow from time to time, although for most papers I read only the first page. So far no scheme has persuaded me to abandon the current one. I discussed two groups of papers before and later changed my mind: first, there is no guarantee of improvement across the board; and, most importantly, I have no need to implement a Workflow in code when I can simply recommend a few open-source SKILLs.

That does not mean multi-Agent development has made no progress; on the contrary, it has made great progress. The cost of multi-Agent work is falling quickly. In particular, once part of the cache can be reused, self-splitting fan-out through `/fork` gives the cost that used to expand rapidly with branches and repeated context at least a chance of being brought much closer to a linear function. A single Agent's capabilities improve only slowly with token efficiency because effective context advances slowly, while growing model intelligence keeps forcing people to look for harder tasks. That is where the real competition among multi-Agent schemes lies: **cost control**.

No model lab has an incentive to drive multi-Agent costs down itself. Unlike model capability, a Workflow spreads quickly: most labs have already open-sourced their harnesses, and a scheme that performs well can propagate within a day. The Workflows that really matter to most users are the ones that drive the cost of a large task to its minimum. A smart model can, to some extent, explore a collaboration scheme by itself, but **the exploration is also a cost**. Writing a local optimum directly into a SKILL and reusing it is more economical for a small number of large tasks. If you have millions of dollars, of course, I strongly recommend exploring it deeply and writing a paper; you might even found a company. But sprawling is not designed to supply that Workflow. I do not have the financial resources to test several trillion tokens against every model and customise an optimal Workflow for it. If I were a Cursor engineer perhaps I could, though in a sense one or two top-tier subscriptions' weekly allowances, whether for GPT or Claude, are enough to explore a Workflow for a private business or professional field — and even that only covers the first 80%. The later iteration and maintenance, supervision by domain experts and feedback from real scenarios are where the greatest costs lie. The goal of sprawling agents, then, is to provide a good platform on which an individual can build and test their own Workflow. I will deal with the irritating performance problems of running at scale and reduce the black boxes at runtime; you bring your expertise and real scenarios, and concentrate on developing the Workflow that suits you best.

The default design of sprawling agents is relatively decentralised: models are **as free as possible** inside their write domains, admission doors and confidentiality boundaries. Conversely, the Mayor, as the observation entrance, has no freedom at all. Think of the Mayor's design as an adapter: it concentrates on telling you the necessary information and conveying your ideas. This is the design intention behind my idea of separating expertise from communication. Current models tend to keep their capabilities close to what you yourself can actually do, which of course comes from the fact that an LLM is fundamentally a one-dimensional token-sequence prediction function. An adapter layer can first translate your idea into professional content for execution, and then let the Mayor translate the result back into “language your grandmother can understand”, buying both clear communication and task-completion ability for a little extra cost. It really is a little extra cost, because you can use a very cheap model as Mayor and register a smaller context window for it, say 256k through `select_model`'s `context_tokens`; context reminders are measured against that figure. This is a setting for the model, not a separate ceiling for the Mayor's seat. You could also use a model such as DeepSeek with a cache lasting close to 24 hours, so the background work can concentrate on finishing the task in one go and the risk of recomputing the cache during a conversation is reduced. Any restriction imposed in advance would become an obstacle to your own customisation.

I believe that much of the code behind the new features in the software we use every day, not just the AI button, is already approaching 100% AI-written; indeed, Agents now generate the overwhelming majority of the code in almost every major company's AI-related products. If you led an AI lab and found your employees writing a product by hand, you might spend one franc's worth of time appreciating their craftsmanship, and the rest of the day in despair at how weak your own model must be if it could not develop the company's own product. Imagine that [the migration of Bun from Zig to Rust used a prerelease Claude Fable 5](https://bun.com/blog/bun-in-rust), and that earlier this year it could already keep fifty-odd dynamic workflows running for eleven days. How many months of difference does that represent?

Unless you approach programming with the mindset of buying credits in a game, I would say you **absolutely should not program by making wishes**. Wishful programming can produce a beautiful demo, but it almost never produces a project that stays in use for a long time. Strictly speaking, if you do not understand what you are designing, you will not be willing to finish the last 10% of software development that AI has not yet accelerated to its limit either. Many projects now are brought into the world but not raised; even projects that become popular can stop being maintained as soon as the attention passes. To some extent, you will not want to keep using them for long either. This is also true of the many projects born in the current age of mass reverse engineering. A paid feature has indeed been unlocked, but a large company's moat is not the product itself — one reason more and more large companies embrace open source. Their compute, marketing, after-sales support, capital, ecosystem, user habits and communities are what open-source maintainers find hardest to obtain. A feature, by contrast, is an inspirational creation and easier for a large company to appropriate, as we have seen again and again throughout history. If the author of an open-source project I need cannot maintain it for practical reasons, and I am unwilling to fork and maintain it or rebuild the wheel myself, the winner in the end is the large company with almost unlimited resources.

From the past to the present, we still have no perfect way to rule out bugs and compatibility problems. AI is lowering the cost for an individual developer to maintain a project, but the effort required has not fallen by nearly as much. Even a major online personality like Theo3, who spent tens of thousands of dollars rewriting tsc in Rust, said he did not intend to maintain it. The “body” of sprawling agent v0.0.1 was tens of thousands of characters of Markdown containing a large number of imagined scenarios and detailed descriptions. The model at the time did not implement it fully or record all of it; much of it remained in my head, and those things in my head will help the coming development avoid some detours. Whenever you ask me whether sprawling agents v0.0.1 is usable, my answer is: do not even try it. I learned something new in every version after that, and went deeper into the details to improve them; the models and my own workflow developed too. I therefore set a goal towards 0.1.0 Beta — I will apply that Beta tag only when I can say this is a good harness and, after being maintained for this long, is worth trying — to make sprawling agents genuinely recommendable.

The difference between a demo and a finished piece of work now lies only in that last 10%, but the difference in experience is like zero and one. It takes countless details, refinements and bug fixes to make a project look as though it has finally gone from zero to one; at present I would place sprawling agent at roughly 0.6. A large number of tsc rewrites based on Claude Opus 5.5 have recently appeared in the TypeScript ecosystem. I am watching how those projects perform, and will wait for a more AI-native, extremely fast frontend ecosystem to mature before pursuing generative UI. For now, though, the approach of writing Svelte + CSS + JavaScript directly has largely settled; in a sense, default components or templates generally perform faster, but models are growing so quickly and everyone has different tastes, so greater openness and freedom may be better.

The project's frontend currently uses Svelte + TypeScript. Once I think its structure has been tuned into a good shape, I might follow the current trend and replace the browser client with a native desktop client, perhaps using [GPUI](https://docs.rs/gpui/latest/gpui/) to migrate the frontend back to Rust. GPUI is still pre-1.0, and its official documentation names macOS and Linux, so Windows support would have to be addressed first. The earliest version of the project used Dioxus for its frontend, but I would still keep [Topcoat](https://github.com/tokio-rs/topcoat) in the WebUI. I moved to the TypeScript ecosystem only because it makes writing and designing with AI convenient, and because of its package managers; the ideal is still for Rust to take over as much as possible. I intend to leave all these decisions until the end of the year or even early next year. This would require not only a sufficiently polished frontend but also a considerable degree of decoupling between dependencies. The WebUI already provides many of the features we need, and I am considering making that one of the conditions for v0.1.0 Beta.

I have recently been very interested in https://github.com/ELY-Open-Source/ElyOffice, and it was this project that started me thinking about GPUI rather than using Tauri directly to keep the current Svelte frontend and carry the system WebView around. If I really did use GPUI, I would prefer it to become the wire's second client, with the WebUI continuing to cover remote access, rather than binding the kernel and interface together again. Another reason to keep the WebUI is that the TUI is currently usable but not especially good, so it does not count as an interface that needs maintaining. If we build a GUI in the future, it could embed a terminal and provide a much better visualisation of tool and terminal commands. Work that needs extensive TUI interaction could use it directly, and someone who dislikes a GUI could still use the TUI inside the emulated terminal — although a terminal is not just a few lines of text either: there is VT parsing, Unicode, selections, scrollback, PTYs and more.

There is also another idea: let the WebUI support a video background, like Wallpaper Engine, or go further and use WebGPU for something more interesting. I know some people urgently want to converse in real time with Rei Ayanami or another anime character they love. Once everything is mature, the interface layer might take only one version to build, but the things underneath it are a complete product effort of their own: consistency of the character's identity and persistent memory, full-duplex voice interaction with voice cloning, control and rendering of a 2D or 3D model, image and video models working together, and — less important in other schemes but exceptionally important in this one — making the whole UI liquid glass.

There is still a long way to go; you are welcome to join the project's development and discussion.

---

**Notes / 补充**

- **Tools / 工具** — An `edit` is admitted by the files the current run has read: a file nobody wrote since that read may be edited, a conflict returns the current passage around `old_string`, and a resumed, forked or delegated run reads before it edits. `old_string: ""` creates a file only where none exists. `exec` takes exactly one of `command` and `python`; where a building has no shell, a command is read as a program and its arguments rather than as shell syntax. `search` matches a regular expression one line at a time, and a `glob` without a pattern lists file names. `tool` provides `list`, `find`, `detail` and `run`.

  `edit` 由当前 run 读过的文件准入：文件在读后没有被别人写过才能编辑；发生冲突时返回 `old_string` 附近的当前内容；续接、分叉或委派的 run 都要先读再改。`old_string: ""` 只在文件不存在时创建它。`exec` 必须且只能给 `command` 或 `python` 之一；楼未启用 shell 时，命令按程序和参数解析，不按 shell 语法执行。`search` 逐行匹配正则表达式，只给 `glob` 时列出文件名。`tool` 提供 `list`、`find`、`detail` 和 `run`。

- **Interface / 界面** — The raise page can build or adopt a folder, and the command palette can carry a conversation to another room. The building page shows the next run's prompt layers and edits each tool's `core` / `dormant` / `off` exposure. The panorama keeps the conversation rather than a second timeline; moments visible on a screen use local time, with the UTC instant retained in `datetime`.

  建楼页可以新建楼或收养已有文件夹，命令面板可以把会话带到另一个房间。楼页展示下一次 run 的提示词层级，并编辑每件工具的 `core`／`dormant`／`off` 暴露。全景保留会话而不再重复一条时间线；屏幕上显示的时刻使用本地时间，UTC 时刻仍保留在 `datetime` 中。

- **Security fixes / 安全修复** — `wasmtime` and `wasmtime-wasi` move to 48.0.7 for GHSA-9pvw-hwfg-92h5 (RUSTSEC-2026-0378); `ctutils`, `rustls-webpki` and `webpki-root-certs` move to 0.4.5, 0.103.16 and 1.0.11 for RUSTSEC-2026-0385, RUSTSEC-2026-0382 and RUSTSEC-2026-0383.

  wasmtime 与 wasmtime-wasi 升到 48.0.7，覆盖 GHSA-9pvw-hwfg-92h5（RUSTSEC-2026-0378）；ctutils、rustls-webpki、webpki-root-certs 分别升到 0.4.5、0.103.16、1.0.11，覆盖 RUSTSEC-2026-0385、RUSTSEC-2026-0382、RUSTSEC-2026-0383。

- **Measurement / 实测** — No release build of 0.0.13 was measured. The 3 ms → 1 ms figures above are an illustration, not a benchmark result; the pull-request readings recorded in the CHANGELOG came from unoptimized builds and are directions rather than release results.

  本版没有发版构建的实测；上文的 3ms→1ms 只是演算假设，不是实测结果。CHANGELOG 记录的 PR 读数来自未优化构建，只能说明方向，不能当作本版发版构建的成绩。

- **Updating / 升级方式** — First make a backup as the [Updating section of getting-started](https://github.com/2youg1/sprawling-agents/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md#updating) describes. Version 0.0.12 kept an unnamed city in `city/` beside the binary. Put the new version in that old folder and run `sprawling` or `sprawling up` without a path: it moves the whole city to `~/sprawling/city`, re-points the worktrees and writes a `city` line into `~/.sprawling/config.toml`, once only. If you unpack the new version elsewhere, it cannot find the old city and the first screen offers to create one at `~/sprawling/city`; type the old city's folder on that screen instead, which writes the `city` line, or use `sprawling up <old-city-folder>` for one launch only. A city on a different volume from the home directory, such as a binary on `D:` and a home directory on `C:`, is not moved: it opens where it is and its original path is written into `city`. Writing that line does not preserve comments or layout in `config.toml`. An `[[mcp]]` server labelled `computer`, `media`, `record`, `skill`, `sprawling` or `web` is now refused with `E_CONFIG_INVALID`, because those namespaces belong to the city's own tools; rename it. Going back to 0.0.12 is not promised: name a moved city with `sprawling up <old-city-folder>`; 0.0.12 does not understand the V2/V3 renderer versions and draws tool results as JSON, so after a downgrade a branched or resumed session shows the model a history different from the one it saw at the time; it also refuses a `CONFIG.toml` carrying `[catalog]`, and the `MAYOR.md` / `CLERK.md` copies brought forward by 0.0.13 no longer contain the `<plan>` / `<seen>` procedure 0.0.12 needs. The last two points were checked against the 0.0.12 source, not run.

  先照 [getting-started 的 Updating 一节](https://github.com/2youg1/sprawling-agents/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md#updating) 做好备份。0.0.12 把没指名的城放在二进制旁边的 `city/` 里。把新版放进那个旧文件夹、不带路径运行 `sprawling` 或 `sprawling up`，它会把城整个搬到 `~/sprawling/city`，把工作树改指新位置，并在 `~/.sprawling/config.toml` 写入 `city` 一行，只搬这一次。新版解压到别的文件夹时找不到旧城，第一屏会提议在 `~/sprawling/city` 新建一座：这时在第一屏输入旧城的文件夹（会写进 `city` 一行），或用 `sprawling up <旧城文件夹>` 只开这一次。旧城和家目录不在同一个卷上（比如二进制在 `D:`、家目录在 `C:`）时不搬，城在原处打开，原路径写进 `city` 一行。写这一行时 `config.toml` 的注释和排版不保留。`[[mcp]]` 里如果有服务器的标签是 `computer`、`media`、`record`、`skill`、`sprawling` 或 `web`，现在会被 `E_CONFIG_INVALID` 拒绝，因为这些是城自己工具的命名空间，请改名。不保证能退回 0.0.12：搬过位置的城要用 `sprawling up <旧城文件夹>` 指名；0.0.12 不认 V2／V3 的渲染版本，会把工具结果画成 JSON，所以退回之后分支或续接的会话里模型看到的历史与它当时看到的不同；带 `[catalog]` 的 `CONFIG.toml` 也会被它拒绝，而新版带过去的 `MAYOR.md`／`CLERK.md` 已没有旧版需要的 `<plan>`／`<seen>` 规程，后两项只核对了旧版源码，未实际运行。

- **Known issue / 已知问题** — ([#185](https://github.com/2youg1/sprawling-agents/issues/185)) On an Anthropic-compatible endpoint, forking a session containing tool calls fails. The Ledger redacts the provider's tool call id as `secret:redacted/<hash>` because of its key-like shape, and the rebuilt history sends it back unchanged; Anthropic requires an id matching `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$`, answers 400, and the run ends cancelled. Version 0.0.12 behaves the same way, so this is not a regression in 0.0.13. An OpenAI-compatible endpoint accepts the id, and a new session is unaffected.

  （[#185](https://github.com/2youg1/sprawling-agents/issues/185)）在 Anthropic 兼容格式的端点上，分叉一个含工具调用的会话会失败。账本把 provider 给的 tool call id 按密钥形状抹成 `secret:redacted/<hash>`，重建历史时原样发出，Anthropic 要求 id 匹配 `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$`，回答 400，run 以 cancelled 结束。0.0.12 就是这样，不是本版的回归；OpenAI 兼容格式的端点接受这个 id，新会话不受影响。

**What comes next** — continued tool and runtime work, a deliberately scoped sandbox design, and exploration of generative UI and a possible second, native client. No version or date is promised for `v0.1.0` Beta, and finishing any item here does not by itself make it.

**Maturity ladder / 成熟度阶梯**

| Stage | Version | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| pre-alpha | 0.0.x | runs end to end; nothing is promised |
| alpha | 0.0.x | usable / 可用 |
| beta | 0.1.0 | good to use / 好用 |
| stable | 1.0.0 | no compromise on experience or on long-term maintenance, with a mature maintainer or team / 体验与长期维护都不妥协，维护者或团队成熟 |
